overview.description: Mexican Train is a popular domino game played mainly in the USA. It is best for four or more players and uses a double-twelve domino set. Players build trains of dominoes from a central hub, with each player having their own personal train and a shared 'Mexican Train' that anyone can play on. The game combines strategic tile placement with careful hand management.

history.origins: Mexican Train originated in the United States, though its exact origins are unclear. Despite the name, it has no confirmed connection to Mexico. The game became popular in the late 20th century.
timeline: Late 20th Century: Emerges in the United States
1990s: Gains popularity as a family game
2000s: Commercial Mexican Train sets become available
Present: One of the most popular domino games in the USA
history.evolution: The game has spawned many variations and house rules. The core mechanic of personal trains plus a shared Mexican Train has remained consistent.
history.cultural: A popular family game in the USA, often played at gatherings and game nights. The simple rules make it accessible to children while offering strategic depth for adults.

setup.deck: Double-twelve domino set (91 tiles with 0-12 pips on each half).
setup.equipment: Double-twelve domino set, train markers (coins or special markers), central hub piece (optional).
setup.dealing: Number of tiles varies by player count: 2 players = 15 each, 3-4 players = 12 each, 5-6 players = 10 each, 7-8 players = 9 each. Remaining tiles form the boneyard.

rules.objective: Be the first player to play all your dominoes, or have the lowest pip count when the game is blocked.
rules.gameplay: Play starts with the highest double (12-12) in the center. Each player has a personal train from the hub; a shared Mexican Train is open to all. On the first turn only, a player may play as many matching tiles as they can on their train. From the second turn onward, each player plays one tile per turn (or more if playing doubles) onto their own train, another player's marked train, or the Mexican Train. If unable to play, the player draws one tile from the boneyard and may play it if it fits; otherwise they pass and place a marker on their train. Exposed doubles must be satisfied by the next player. The first player to play all tiles wins the round; otherwise the player with fewest pips in hand wins when blocked.
keyRules: Start with highest double in center
Each player has a personal train
Mexican Train is shared by all
Lowest pip count wins if blocked

strategy.basic: Try to play your highest pip tiles early. Start your train as soon as possible. Play on the Mexican Train when you don't have plays for your own train.
strategy.intermediate: Manage your doubles carefully - they can help you control the game but require immediate attention. Force opponents to mark their trains by controlling available plays.
strategy.advanced: Track which tiles have been played to predict opponents' holdings. Use doubles strategically to force opponents to draw. Time your plays to leave yourself with exit options.
tips: Don't hold too many high-pip tiles - they hurt if someone else goes out
Playing a double can be a defensive move to slow down the game
If you have multiple plays, choose the one that leaves you with the most options
Watch opponents' trains to predict what tiles they might need

difficulty.medium: Prioritizes high pip tiles; understands double strategy; basic tile tracking.

play_card.description: Play one domino onto your train, another player's marked train, or the Mexican Train so the inward end matches the open end of the layout. On first turn only you may play multiple tiles forming a valid train. Playing a double requires an extra tile (can go anywhere allowed); multiple doubles require one tile per double.
play_card.constraints: Tile end must match the open end of the target train. You may only play on your train, a train marked with a penny, or the Mexican Train. You must play if you have a legal move.

draw.description: Draw one tile from the boneyard when you have no legal play. If the drawn tile is playable you must play it.
draw.constraints: Only when you have no legal play; boneyard must have tiles. You may not draw if you had a playable tile. After drawing, if the tile is playable you must play it.
